items.title: Rows for five letters
items.prose: A risk alert depends on five conditions, $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$ and $T$. Each is either T or F.
items.question: How many rows does the alert's full truth table need?

feedback.correct: $2^5 = 32$ rows: each new letter doubles the count.
feedback.generic: Each letter has two values, and the choices multiply.

byKey.times: You multiplied 2 by 5 to get 10. Each new letter doubles the rows, so it is $2^5$.
byKey.square: You took $5^2 = 25$. The base is the two truth values, so it is $2^5$.

explain.text: One letter gives 2 rows, and each extra letter doubles them. Five letters give $2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2 = 32$.

items.title: A rule nobody triggered
items.prose: Rule: **if a trade is over £2m, it is reported by noon**. Today the desk made one trade, of £500,000, reported at 3pm.
items.question: Was the rule kept today?

options.text: Yes. The trade was not over £2m, so the rule asked nothing of it.
No. The trade was reported after noon.
options.why: You checked the conclusion alone. The rule only binds trades over £2m.

options.text: Neither. With no trade over £2m the rule has no truth value today.
options.why: You treated a false hypothesis as leaving the rule undefined. An implication with a false hypothesis is true.

options.text: No. A trade reported after noon must have been over £2m.
options.why: You read the rule backwards. That is its converse, which the rule does not claim.

feedback.correct: The hypothesis is false, so the implication is true: the rule was kept.
feedback.generic: An implication fails only when its hypothesis is true and its conclusion false.

explain.text: $P \Rightarrow Q$ is false only on the row where $P$ is T and $Q$ is F. Here $P$, over £2m, is F. So the rule holds today, vacuously.

items.title: Counting elements
items.question: What is $|X|$, the number of elements of $X$?

feedback.correct: The elements are $2$, $\{2, 3\}$ and $\{3\}$, so $|X| = 3$.
feedback.generic: List the distinct objects between the outer braces. A set inside counts as one object.

byKey.repeat: You counted the repeated 2 twice, giving 4. Repeats do not add elements.
byKey.flatten: You counted the numbers 2 and 3 inside. $\{2, 3\}$ and $\{3\}$ are each one element.

explain.text: The outer braces hold $2$, $\{2, 3\}$, $\{3\}$ and $2$ again. The repeat adds nothing. Each inner set is one element, so $|X| = 3$.

items.title: Callable or floating
items.prose: A book holds 40 bonds. 22 are callable, 17 pay a floating rate, and 9 are both.
items.question: How many bonds are callable or floating, or both?

feedback.generic: Add the two counts, then take off the bonds counted twice.

byKey.added: You added 22 and 17 to get 39. The 9 bonds that are both were counted twice.
byKey.twice: You took off the overlap twice. It was counted twice, so remove it once.

explain.text: $|C \cup F| = |C| + |F| - |C \cap F|$, since the overlap sits in both counts. That gives $22 + 17 - 9 = 30$, and $40 - 30 = 10$ bonds are neither.

items.title: Name the witness
items.prose: Consider $\exists x \in \mathbb{Z},\ 4x + 7 = -5$.
items.question: What is the witness $x$?

feedback.correct: $4x = -12$, so $x = -3$, an integer. The claim is true.
feedback.generic: Take 7 from both sides, then divide by 4.

byKey.added: You added 7 instead of taking it away. Also, 0.5 is not in $\mathbb{Z}$.

explain.text: An existential claim needs one value that works. $4(-3) + 7 = -5$, and $-3 \in \mathbb{Z}$. So $x = -3$ is the witness.

items.title: The opposite of a rota rule
items.prose: Claim: **every desk that trades FX has a trader on call every night**.
items.question: Which sentence is its negation?

options.text: Some desk trades FX and has a night with no trader on call.
No desk that trades FX has a trader on call on any night.
options.why: You negated every part and kept the quantifiers. Each quantifier must flip.

options.text: Some desk that does not trade FX has a trader on call every night.
options.why: You negated the hypothesis. $\lnot(P \Rightarrow Q)$ keeps $P$ and negates $Q$.

options.text: Every desk that trades FX has some night with no trader on call.
options.why: You kept the first "every". The negation needs only one desk that fails.

feedback.correct: Some FX desk has a night with no one on call. That one desk breaks the claim.
feedback.generic: Flip each quantifier in place, and negate the implication as $P$ and not $Q$.

explain.text: The outer "every desk" becomes "some desk", which must still trade FX. Inside, "every night" becomes "some night" with no one on call. One such desk breaks the claim.

items.title: The inverse and the negation
items.prose: The column $P \Rightarrow Q$ is given. Fill the inverse $\lnot P \Rightarrow \lnot Q$ and the column $P \land \lnot Q$.
items.question: Fill both columns with T or F.

feedback.correct: $P \land \lnot Q$ is the opposite of $P \Rightarrow Q$ on every row. The inverse matches the converse instead.
feedback.generic: An implication is F only where its hypothesis is T and its conclusion F. An "and" is T only where both parts are T.

byKey.ft-inverse: On the F, T row, $\lnot P$ is T and $\lnot Q$ is F, so the inverse is F.
byKey.imp-not-ft: You read it as $P \Rightarrow \lnot Q$. An "and" is T only when both parts are T.
byKey.imp-not-ff: You read it as $P \Rightarrow \lnot Q$. An "and" is T only when both parts are T.

explain.text: The inverse reads T, T, F, T, the same as the converse, not as $P \Rightarrow Q$. $P \land \lnot Q$ reads F, T, F, F, the opposite of $P \Rightarrow Q$ on every row. So it is the negation of the implication.

items.title: Routing three orders
items.prose: Each of 3 orders is sent to one of 4 venues. Several orders may go to the same venue.
items.question: How many functions from the orders to the venues are there?

feedback.correct: Each order has 4 choices, so there are $4^3 = 64$ functions.
feedback.generic: A function picks one venue for each order. Multiply the choices.

byKey.swapped: You took $3^4 = 81$. That gives each venue one of 3 orders, which is a function the other way.
byKey.product: You took $3 \times 4 = 12$. That counts the (order, venue) pairs, not the functions.

explain.text: A function gives every order exactly one venue. Order 1, order 2 and order 3 each have 4 choices. So there are $4 \times 4 \times 4 = 64$.

items.title: Three analysts, six sectors
items.prose: Three analysts are each given one of 6 sectors to cover. No two analysts share a sector.
items.question: How many such one-to-one functions are there?

feedback.correct: $6 \times 5 \times 4 = 120$: each analyst has one fewer sector left.
feedback.generic: The first analyst has 6 choices, the next has one fewer, and so on.

byKey.any: You took $6^3 = 216$. That lets two analysts share a sector, so it is not one-to-one.
byKey.unordered: You counted the 20 sets of 3 sectors. Which analyst gets which sector matters.

explain.text: One-to-one means no sector is used twice. The choices fall from 6 to 5 to 4. That gives $120$ functions.

items.title: Lots from a bill
items.prose: A broker charges a fixed £2.50 plus £0.80 a lot: $c(n) = 2.5 + 0.8n$. It is one-to-one, so it has an inverse on its image.
items.question: A bill reads £14.50. How many lots were traded?

feedback.generic: Undo the steps in reverse: take off the fixed £2.50, then divide by £0.80.

byKey.forward: You worked out $c(14.5) = 14.1$. The bill is an output, so apply $c^{-1}$.
byKey.added: You added the £2.50, giving 21.25. Undoing $+2.5$ means taking it away.

explain.text: $c$ multiplies by 0.8 and then adds 2.5. The inverse undoes them in reverse: subtract 2.5, then divide by 0.8. $(14.5 - 2.5) / 0.8 = 12 / 0.8 = 15$.

items.title: Growth factors
items.prose: A price is multiplied by $g(x) = e^x$ when its natural log rises by $x$. Take $g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$.
items.question: Which describes $g$?

options.text: One-to-one but not onto: no $x$ gives $g(x) = -1$.
One-to-one and onto, since $\ln$ undoes it.
options.why: You took $\ln$ as a full inverse. $\ln y$ exists only for $y > 0$, so negative targets have no $x$.

options.text: Onto but not one-to-one.
options.why: You swapped the two tests. $e^a = e^b$ forces $a = b$, so it is one-to-one.

options.text: Neither one-to-one nor onto.
options.why: You saw that $-1$ is never reached and stopped there. $e^a = e^b$ still forces $a = b$, so $g$ is one-to-one.

feedback.correct: $e^a = e^b$ gives $a = b$, but every output is positive, so $-1$ has no preimage.
feedback.generic: Check one-to-one with $g(a) = g(b)$. For onto, find an output of $\mathbb{R}$ that is never reached.

explain.text: Taking $\ln$ of $e^a = e^b$ gives $a = b$, so $g$ is one-to-one. But $e^x > 0$ for every $x$, so $y = -1$ is never reached. With codomain $(0, \infty)$ it would be onto.

items.title: Chasing an element
items.prose: Claim: $(A \cup B) \cap C \subseteq (A \cap C) \cup B$ for all sets $A$, $B$, $C$.
items.question: Put the proof in order. Two lines do not belong: move them to Left out.

lines.text: Let $x \in (A \cup B) \cap C$.
Then $x \in C$, and $x \in A$ or $x \in B$.
If $x \in A$, then $x \in A \cap C$, since $x \in C$.
If $x \in B$, then $x$ is in the right side already.
In either case $x \in (A \cap C) \cup B$.
So every element of the left side is in the right side. $\blacksquare$
Then $x \in A$, $x \in B$ and $x \in C$.
lines.why: You turned "or" into "and". $x \in A \cup B$ only says $x$ is in at least one of them.

lines.text: Take $A = \{1\}$, $B = \varnothing$, $C = \{1\}$: both sides are $\{1\}$.
lines.why: You kept an example. One case is evidence, not a step of the proof.

feedback.correct: Pick an element, unpack the definitions, split into the two cases and repack.
feedback.generic: Start from an element of the left side, then use the meaning of $\cup$ and $\cap$.

byKey.d1: You kept the line that turns "or" into "and". Split into cases instead.
byKey.d2: You kept the example. It checks one case and proves nothing for all sets.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: Subset means every element of the left side lies in the right. The "or" in $A \cup B$ forces two cases. The cases may come in either order.

items.title: Odd, odd, odd
items.prose: Claim: if $m$ and $n$ are odd, then $mn + m + n$ is odd. Write $m = 2a + 1$ and $n = 2b + 1$ for integers $a$ and $b$.
items.question: Which line finishes the proof?

options.text: $mn + m + n = 4ab + 4a + 4b + 3 = 2(2ab + 2a + 2b + 1) + 1$, twice an integer plus 1.
Write $m = n = 2k + 1$. Then $mn + m + n = 4k^2 + 8k + 3 = 2(2k^2 + 4k + 1) + 1$, which is odd.
options.why: You used one letter for both numbers. That proves only the case $m = n$.
You checked two cases. The claim is about every pair of odd numbers.

options.text: $mn + m + n = 4ab + 4a + 4b + 3$, and 4 is even, so the total is odd.
options.why: You stopped before the form $2(\text{integer}) + 1$. Saying "4 is even" does not reach the definition of odd.

feedback.correct: $4ab + 4a + 4b + 3 = 2(2ab + 2a + 2b + 1) + 1$, which is odd by definition.
feedback.generic: Expand with separate letters for $m$ and $n$, then write the result as $2(\text{integer}) + 1$.

explain.text: Two odd numbers need two letters, $a$ and $b$, or the proof covers only $m = n$. Expanding gives $4ab + 4a + 4b + 3$. Taking out 2 leaves the form that defines odd.

items.title: Average and best quarter
items.prose: Claim: **if a fund's average return over four quarters is above 3%, then some quarter returned above 3%**. We prove it by contrapositive.
items.question: Which statement do we prove?

options.text: If every quarter returned at most 3%, the average is at most 3%.
If some quarter returned above 3%, the average is above 3%.
options.why: You swapped hypothesis and conclusion. That is the converse, and it is false: one good quarter is not enough.

options.text: If the average is at most 3%, every quarter returned at most 3%.
options.why: You negated both parts but kept their order. That is the inverse, which says something different.

options.text: The average is above 3% and every quarter returned at most 3%.
options.why: You wrote the negation of the claim. That is what a proof by contradiction assumes.

feedback.correct: $\lnot Q \Rightarrow \lnot P$: no quarter above 3% forces the average to be at most 3%.
feedback.generic: Negate the conclusion, then show the negated hypothesis follows.

explain.text: The contrapositive is easy to prove: four returns each at most 3% sum to at most 12%. Dividing by 4 gives an average of at most 3%. That proves the claim.

items.title: Rational plus irrational
items.prose: Claim: if $a$ is rational and $b$ is irrational, then $a + b$ is irrational. We prove it by contradiction.
items.question: Which argument is a correct proof?

options.text: Suppose $a + b = s$ with $s$ rational. Then $b = s - a$ is a difference of rationals, so rational, a contradiction.
Take $a = 1$ and $b = \sqrt{2}$. Then $1 + \sqrt{2}$ is irrational.
options.why: You argued from one pair. The proof must cover every rational $a$ and irrational $b$.

options.text: Suppose $a + b$ is irrational. Then $b = (a + b) - a$ is irrational, as required.
options.why: You assumed the conclusion. A contradiction proof assumes its opposite, that $a + b$ is rational.

options.text: Suppose $a + b$ is rational. A sum is rational only when both parts are, so $b$ is rational.
options.why: You used a false rule: $\sqrt{2} + (1 - \sqrt{2}) = 1$ is rational. Write $b = s - a$ instead.

feedback.correct: Assume $a + b$ is rational. Then $b = (a + b) - a$ is rational, against the hypothesis.
feedback.generic: Assume the opposite of the conclusion, then solve for $b$.

explain.text: The opposite of the conclusion is "$a + b$ is rational". Rationals are closed under subtraction, so $b = (a + b) - a$ is rational. That contradicts $b$ being irrational.

items.title: A step with nothing under it
items.prose: Claim: $n + 1 < n$ for every whole number $n \ge 1$. Step: assume $k + 1 < k$. Adding 1 gives $k + 2 < k + 1$.
items.question: The step is valid. What does the argument show?

options.text: Nothing. The base case fails, since $1 + 1 < 1$ is false, so the chain never starts.
The claim is true, since the step works for every $k$.
options.why: You skipped the base case. A step only carries truth forward from a case that holds.

options.text: The claim fails at $n = 1$ but holds from $n = 2$, since the step carries it on.
options.why: You let the step carry truth from a false case. At $n = 2$ the claim reads $3 < 2$, also false.

options.text: The claim holds for every large enough $n$.
options.why: You read the step as eventual truth. With no true case to start from, the step proves nothing.

feedback.correct: The step is sound, but there is no true case for it to start from.
feedback.generic: Induction needs both parts. Check the base case.

explain.text: A valid step says: if case $k$ holds, case $k + 1$ holds. At $n = 1$ the claim reads $2 < 1$, which is false. So nothing is ever passed along, and the claim is false for every $n$.

items.title: Which way round
items.prose: A write-up reads: "Claim: if $n^2$ is a multiple of 4, then $n$ is a multiple of 4. Proof: let $n = 4k$. Then $n^2 = 16k^2 = 4(4k^2)$, a multiple of 4. $\blacksquare$"
items.question: What is wrong with it?

options.text: It proves the converse. The claim itself is false: $n = 2$ gives $n^2 = 4$.
Nothing. It starts from the definition and reaches a multiple of 4.
options.why: You checked each line but not the direction. The proof assumes the conclusion and reaches the hypothesis.

options.text: It should write $n^2 = 4k$ and $n = 4m$ with two letters.
options.why: You fixed a style point. The fault is which statement was proved, not the letters.

options.text: A claim about every $n$ needs induction.
options.why: You picked a method by the word "every". The claim is false, so no method proves it.

feedback.correct: The proof shows $4 \mid n \Rightarrow 4 \mid n^2$, the converse. $n = 2$ refutes the claim.
feedback.generic: Compare what the proof assumes with the claim's hypothesis.

explain.text: The claim's hypothesis is about $n^2$, but the proof starts from $n = 4k$. So it proves the converse. A reader who checks the first line against the claim sees it at once, and $n = 2$ refutes the claim.

items.title: A value that lands on a square
items.prose: Claim: for every whole number $n \ge 1$, the number $10n^2 + 1$ is not a perfect square. It gives 11, 41, 91 for $n = 1, 2, 3$.
items.question: What is the smallest $n$ that refutes the claim?

feedback.correct: At $n = 6$ the value is $10 \times 36 + 1 = 361 = 19^2$, a perfect square. Every $n$ from 1 to 5 gives a non-square.
feedback.generic: Work out $10n^2 + 1$ for $n = 4, 5, 6, \dots$ and ask whether each value is a square.

byKey.value: 361 is the value at the counterexample. The question asks for $n$, which is 6.
byKey.root: 19 is the square root of the value. The question asks for $n$, which is 6.
byKey.early: At $n = 5$ the value is 251, which lies between $15^2 = 225$ and $16^2 = 256$. Try one more.

explain.text: The values for $n = 1$ to 5 are 11, 41, 91, 161 and 251, and none is a square. At $n = 6$ the value is $360 + 1 = 361 = 19^2$. One failure refutes the "for every".

items.title: Where the chain can start
items.prose: We want to prove $2^n \ge 7n$ for every whole number $n \ge n_0$, by induction. The step is: if $2^k \ge 7k$ then $2^{k+1} \ge 14k \ge 7k + 7$, which needs $k \ge 1$.
items.question: What is the smallest whole number $n_0$ for which the claim holds for every $n \ge n_0$?

feedback.correct: $2^6 = 64 \ge 42$, and the step works for every $k \ge 1$. At $n = 5$, $32 < 35$.
feedback.generic: Find the first $n$ from which the inequality holds, then check the step covers every case after it.

byKey.zero: $2^0 = 1 \ge 0$ is true, but $n = 1$ gives $2 < 7$. The chain breaks at once.
byKey.five: At $n = 5$, $2^5 = 32$ and $7 \times 5 = 35$, so the base case fails.

explain.text: The inequality fails for $n$ from 1 to 5: at 5, $32 < 35$. At 6, $64 \ge 42$, and the step holds for $k \ge 1$. So $n_0 = 6$; the true case at $n = 0$ does not start a chain.

items.title: A logarithm that is not a fraction
items.prose: Claim: $\log_2 3$ is irrational. Suppose $\log_2 3 = \tfrac{p}{q}$ with $p$ and $q$ positive integers. Then $2^{p/q} = 3$, so $2^p = 3^q$.
items.question: Which fact finishes the proof by contradiction?

options.text: $2^p$ is even, since $p \ge 1$, but $3^q$ is odd, so they cannot be equal.
$p$ and $q$ then share a factor, against lowest terms.
options.why: You copied the $\sqrt{2}$ template. Nothing here makes $p$ and $q$ share a factor; parity does the work.

options.text: $2^p > 3^q$ for all positive $p$ and $q$.
options.why: You compared sizes, as if one side must be bigger. $2^1 < 3^1$ but $2^2 > 3^1$, so size settles nothing.

options.text: $q$ cannot be 0, so the fraction is undefined.
options.why: You named a side condition. $q \ge 1$ was assumed; it is not the contradiction.

feedback.correct: An even number cannot equal an odd one, so no such $p$ and $q$ exist.
feedback.generic: Compare $2^p$ and $3^q$: what is true of every power of 2 that is false of every power of 3?

explain.text: Every positive power of 2 is even and every power of 3 is odd. So $2^p = 3^q$ is impossible. The assumption that $\log_2 3$ is a fraction must be false.

items.title: Write it forwards
items.prose: Claim: for every real $x > 0$, $x + \tfrac{1}{x} \ge 2$. We found the proof by working back from the claim. Now write it forwards.
items.question: Put the proof in order. Two lines do not belong: move them to Left out.

lines.text: Let $x > 0$.
$(x - 1)^2 \ge 0$, since no square is negative.
Expanding, $x^2 - 2x + 1 \ge 0$, so $x^2 + 1 \ge 2x$.
Dividing by $x$, which is positive so the sign is kept, $x + \tfrac{1}{x} \ge 2$. $\blacksquare$
Assume $x + \tfrac{1}{x} \ge 2$. Multiplying by $x$ gives $(x - 1)^2 \ge 0$, which is true.
lines.why: You kept the backward chain. Starting from the claim and reaching a truth proves nothing.
You kept a check of one value. It is evidence, not a step.

feedback.correct: Start from a fact the reader accepts, a square is never negative, and end at the claim.
feedback.generic: A proof runs from accepted facts to the claim, each step with its reason.

byKey.d1: You kept the line that assumes the claim. Write the chain from the square to the claim instead.
byKey.d2: You kept the check at $x = 2$. It covers one value only.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: Working back from the claim is how we found the proof, but it assumes what we want. The forward version starts from $(x - 1)^2 \ge 0$. Dividing by $x > 0$ keeps the direction of $\ge$.

items.title: Products of neighbours
items.prose: Claim: $1 \cdot 2 + 2 \cdot 3 + \dots + n(n + 1) = \tfrac{n(n + 1)(n + 2)}{3}$ for every $n \ge 1$. It holds at $n = 1$: $2 = \tfrac{1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3}{3}$.
items.question: Use the formula, then check its step.

feedback.generic: Put $n = 20$ into $\tfrac{n(n + 1)(n + 2)}{3}$.

byKey.squares: That is $1^2 + \dots + 20^2 = 2{,}870$. Each term here is $i(i + 1)$, one more factor than $i^2$.

parts.question: Step: assume the sum to $k$ terms is $\tfrac{k(k + 1)(k + 2)}{3}$. Which line comes next?

options.why: You added the $k$th term again. The next term is the $(k + 1)$th, $(k + 1)(k + 2)$.

options.text: Assume the formula for every $n$, so it holds at $n = k + 1$.
options.why: You assumed the claim itself. The step may use only case $k$.

options.text: Check $k = 20$: both sides are 3,080, so the step holds.
options.why: You checked one case. The step must work for every $k$.

feedback.correct: Taking out $(k + 1)(k + 2)$ leaves $\tfrac{k}{3} + 1 = \tfrac{k + 3}{3}$, the formula at $k + 1$.
feedback.generic: Add the next term, $(k + 1)(k + 2)$, and take out the common factor.

explain.text: The $(k + 1)$th term is $(k + 1)(k + 2)$. Taking it out as a factor leaves $\tfrac{k}{3} + 1 = \tfrac{k + 3}{3}$. That is the formula with $n = k + 1$, so with the base case it holds for every $n$.

items.title: Not a sum of two squares
items.prose: Claim: no integer of the form $4m + 3$ is a sum of two squares $a^2 + b^2$, for integers $a$ and $b$.
items.question: Put the proof in order. Two lines do not belong: move them to Left out.

lines.text: Suppose $4m + 3 = a^2 + b^2$ for some integers $m$, $a$ and $b$.
If $a = 2j$, then $a^2 = 4j^2$, which leaves remainder 0 on division by 4.
If $a = 2j + 1$, then $a^2 = 4(j^2 + j) + 1$, which leaves remainder 1.
The same holds for $b^2$, so $a^2 + b^2$ leaves remainder 0, 1 or 2.
But $4m + 3$ leaves remainder 3: a contradiction. So no such $a$ and $b$ exist. $\blacksquare$
The same holds for $b^2$, so $a^2 + b^2$ leaves remainder 0 or 1.
lines.why: You dropped the case where both squares leave 1. Then the sum leaves 2.

lines.text: Check 3, 7, 11 and 15: none is a sum of two squares.
lines.why: You kept a list of cases. Four checks cannot cover every $m$.

feedback.correct: Each square leaves 0 or 1 on division by 4. A sum of two leaves 0, 1 or 2, never 3.
feedback.generic: Work out what a square leaves on division by 4, for even and odd bases.

byKey.d1: You kept the line that forgets $1 + 1 = 2$. The sum can leave 0, 1 or 2.
byKey.d2: You kept the checks of four numbers. The claim covers every $m$.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: Split each base into even and odd: squares leave 0 or 1 on division by 4. Two of them sum to 0, 1 or 2. None of those is 3, so the assumed equation is impossible.

items.title: A written induction
items.prompt:
Prove that for every whole number $n \ge 1$,

$$1 \cdot 2^1 + 2 \cdot 2^2 + 3 \cdot 2^3 + \dots + n \cdot 2^n = (n - 1)2^{n + 1} + 2.$$

Write it so a stranger can check every step. State the method, the base case and what the step assumes. Then check the formula at $n = 4$ by adding the terms.
items.model:
We use induction on $n$.

**Base case.** At $n = 1$ the left side is $1 \cdot 2 = 2$. The right side is $0 \cdot 2^2 + 2 = 2$.

**Step.** Assume, for one fixed $k \ge 1$, that $1 \cdot 2^1 + \dots + k \cdot 2^k = (k - 1)2^{k + 1} + 2$. Adding the next term, $(k + 1)2^{k + 1}$, the sum to $k + 1$ terms is

$$(k - 1)2^{k + 1} + 2 + (k + 1)2^{k + 1} = 2k \cdot 2^{k + 1} + 2 = k \cdot 2^{k + 2} + 2.$$

That is $((k + 1) - 1)2^{(k + 1) + 1} + 2$, the formula with $n = k + 1$.

**Conclusion.** The base case holds and each case gives the next. So the formula holds for every $n \ge 1$. $\blacksquare$

**Check at $n = 4$.** $2 + 8 + 24 + 64 = 98$, and $3 \times 2^5 + 2 = 98$.

rubric.text: Names induction on $n$ as the method
Base case: both sides equal 2 at $n = 1$
States the assumption for one fixed $k$, not for every $n$
Adds the next term $(k + 1)2^{k + 1}$ and collects to $2k \cdot 2^{k + 1} + 2$
Rewrites it as $k \cdot 2^{k + 2} + 2$ and says this is the formula at $k + 1$
Concludes for every $n \ge 1$ from the base case and the step
Checks $n = 4$: the terms sum to 98, and $3 \times 32 + 2 = 98$
